issues.legal_issue: A Hindu woman who possesses property given in recognition of her right to maintenance acquires full ownership of it even if no separate restricted estate or right to alienate is shown.
material_facts: A husband entrusted land to his wife and stated that its produce would provide for her maintenance.
The correspondence between the spouses established that the land was given in lieu of maintenance.
The wife relied on the land and its produce, and the purchaser sought to restrain her from interfering with possession.
The High Court held that the wife had only been allowed to use the land’s proceeds for day-to-day expenses and had acquired no limited interest in the land.
issues.conclusion: The land was given to the wife in lieu of maintenance, and her maintenance right was sufficient title for her possession to mature into full ownership. The distinction between day-to-day expenses and maintenance was erroneous; the judgment recognizing her full ownership was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with its Explanation, enlarges into full ownership a Hindu woman’s interest in property possessed by her where that possession has a lawful origin, including property acquired in lieu of maintenance. Her pre-existing right to maintenance is sufficient title; she need not establish a further title or prove a separately granted restricted estate. Section 14(2) is an exception and does not govern acquisitions traceable to an antecedent right. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, Badri Pershad v. Kanso Devi, Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, Sellammal v. Nellammal, Santhanam v. Subramanya, and Krishna Das v. Venkayya, and distinguished Eramma v. Verrupanna.

issues.legal_issue: The exception for property acquired under an instrument prescribing a restricted estate does not displace full ownership where the acquisition recognizes a pre-existing right to maintenance.
material_facts: The husband’s letter entrusted the land to his wife and identified its produce as a source of her maintenance.
The wife had a pre-existing right to maintenance, and the Court found that the land had been given in recognition of that right.
The purchaser argued that the wife had to establish a limited estate without a right of alienation for the statutory enlargement to apply.
issues.conclusion: A separate showing that the wife received a restricted estate was unnecessary. The acquisition was traceable to her pre-existing maintenance right, so the restriction exception did not prevent her interest from becoming full ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property acquired in recognition of a pre-existing right to maintenance is enlarged into full ownership. Section 14(2), which concerns property acquired under a written instrument, decree, order, or award prescribing a restricted estate, is in the nature of an exception and applies where the acquisition is for the first time without a pre-existing right. The Court relied on Badri Pershad v. Kanso Devi, distinguished Naraini Devi v. Rano Devi, and applied the principles in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi and Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai.
